audio_caption: The audio begins with a welcoming introduction, as a male speaker introduces "astronomy with Mr. Gerwin," announcing that they will be exploring the moon. The speaker maintains a clear and informative tone, highlighting the visual aids that will be discussed, such as a 3D model of the moon and what can be seen using the naked eye, telescopes, and space probes. The speaker then refers to the model and indicates the possibility to explore it in detail, with a link shared in the video description.

The audio features a male speaker presenting information about the moon's size and shape, stating "the moon is only about a third as large as the earth" and that "gravity tries to pull it into a sphere." His tone is informative and educational. As he describes the moon's diameter at the equator being slightly larger than across the poles, he adds parenthetically, "not noticeable to the naked eye." Finally, there is a sound.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker describing the moon's orbit around the Earth, mentioning its distance and variability, and explaining the phenomenon of a supermoon. The speaker sounds informative and conversational, concluding by stating that the distance to the moon is on the exam fact sheet. This speech is followed by the distinct sound of a single plucked string instrument, possibly a guitar, marking a transition in the audio.

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker discussing lunar features, mentioning that some are visible "with the naked eye" and others require telescopes or binoculars. He then says "we can see several craters with the naked eye". The speaking tone is informative.

The audio clip features a single, male speaker describing how craters are formed, specifically on the moon, mentioning impact craters, shockwaves, and debris in the context of lunar geology. The speaker adopts a factual and informative tone. This speech is followed by a sound effect.

The audio clip features a single male speaker with a clear, informative tone, discussing the light and dark patches on the moon, which he says are sometimes seen as shapes like a man or a woman. He explains that the light patches, called "terrae" or highlands, are older and thicker, accumulating more craters. He notes that the far side of the moon is almost entirely terrae.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker explaining the dark patches on the moon, known as "maria" or "seas," and dispelling the misconception that they are covered in water. He details how they are lowlands formed by magma eruptions and notes they have fewer craters than "terrae." He mentions these "maria" are predominantly on the near side of the moon, as the crust is thinner there. Finally, he advises that while "maria" or "seas" are acceptable terms, "oceans" is not, when asked in exam. At the end of the audio clip, the speaker trails off.

The audio begins with a male speaker stating that "mountains and valleys are easy to identify." He explains that while they resemble those on Earth, the moon's are formed by asteroid impacts and then he mentions "rills" and "wrinkle ridges," elaborating that these features are not required for the GCSE exam. He lists the seven moon features required for the GCSE exam, giving advice to "think about turning the exam paper" to match memory. The audio ends with the presenter informing you to look at a picture of the moon and with the audio fading to a new sound.

The clip features one male speaker explaining that we only see one side of the moon because it rotates and revolves around the Earth in roughly the same amount of time, keeping the same side facing us, speaking in a conversational tone. The clip then ends with a single chime sound.

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker, conveying information about the moon, emphasizing that "nobody knew what the other side of the moon looked like" until the Russians sent Luna 3 to take photographs in 1959. His tone is informative and slightly academic, highlighting the differences between the near and far sides of the moon, and explaining that the near side has more maria and fewer craters. The speaker mentions plans for a video on the moon's origin and structure, promising to elaborate on the reasons behind the characteristics.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker providing information about the moon, specifically mentioning that "the period of the moon's rotation is the same as the period of its orbit." He emphasizes remembering a specific number, "27.3 days," as it may be required on an exam. The speaker then questions, "But why are they the same?".

The audio clip begins with a clear, informative male voice explaining that "this is down to an effect called tidal locking" and that "the Earth's gravity pulls the near side of the moon more strongly than the far side", describing the process over time. The tone is educational and steady. He continues that, "the moon is doing the same to the earth, but much slower." He concludes that most moons are tidally locked to their host planet.

The clip begins with a single male speaker explaining that without space probes, we'd assume we see 50% of the moon, but that's not quite true. He adopts a conversational tone, suggesting the listener get a ball and move closer and further away from it to demonstrate why we can see slightly less than 50%. He then states that this is still not the whole story. Finally, we hear a short, musical interlude.

The audio clip starts with a calm, educational-sounding male voice explaining the effect called "libration" which has three varieties. He references moving across the earth, shifting angles of sight, peaking around the edges, and shows the moon viewed at the same time from different latitudes. He also describes how as the earth rotates, one can "peek around the sides," which he defines as "diurnal libration." This section of speech is then followed by a science fiction-esque ambient music with electronic tones. Finally, a male voice resumes, stating that the video shows two other types of libration occurring throughout the month.

The audio clip features a single male speaker explaining two types of "libration" of the moon, first "libration in longitude" due to its elliptical orbit, then "libration in latitude" due to its tilted axis. The speaker maintains a calm, informative tone throughout the explanation.

The audio clip features one male speaker discussing the visibility of the moon's surface from Earth, stating that "With all of these effects combined, we can see a total of 59% of the Moon's surface from Earth." He notes that "For the rest, we need spacecraft." The speaker's tone is informative and matter-of-fact.

The audio clip begins with a speaker, who sounds like a man, summarizing the content of a video, mentioning the diameter, distance, rotation, and orbital period of the moon. He states there will be two more videos about the moon, discussing phases, eclipses, and tides, as well as the moon's origin, internal structure, and the Apollo missions. The speaker then says thank you and goodbye in a positive tone. This is followed by a low, humming sound.
